Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Nothing says true love like releasing a caged butterfly, don't you think? Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin are to be paid $5 million for the picture rights to their wedding. The butterflies are reported to be the piece-de-resistance of England's most anticipated celebrity wedding of the year. Wayne Rooney, the best English footballer of his generation, and Coleen McLoughlin, his High School sweetheart, were to marry in an estimated $10 million ceremony in Italy Thursday. As they kiss, guests are apparently meant to open boxes and release the butterflies. The moment has been pilloried widely in the British media, tacky and over the top they all think, but is it just sour grapes? It has been a long and, at times, bumpy road for the couple to the altar. One littered with fierce criticism from the British press, which has enjoyed nothing more than lampooning Rooney and McLoughlin for being 'common.' The Daily Mail once even asked: "Is this Britain's ghastliest couple?" Rooney has been dubbed "Shrek" and "Mr Potato Head" due to his looks and his background as the son of a school dinner lady who grew up on a council estate is often referred to in a disparaging way. McLoughlin, meanwhile, has been subjected to page upon page of bitter stories about her weight, shopping sprees and her lack of closeness to Victoria Beckham. There has also been fierce criticism over the fact she has managed to become a millionaire in her own right. It's all down to Rooney apparently, and nothing to do with her appearing to be quite a decent person, who did well at school and has cleverly managed to parlay some of her fame into various media and advertising projects. Anyone who has seen her television show -- Coleen's Real Women -- can see she is a decent, bubbly person, who is very good at putting people at ease. Much to the media's fury, the couple have sold the rights to cover the wedding to OK magazine for a record $5 million. However they're not pocketing all the cash themselves, with an undisclosed sum from the fee to be donated to the Claire House children's hospice in Cheshire -- where McLoughlin's disabled foster sister Rosie is cared for. The queen's grandson, Peter Phillips and his bride Autumn Kelly, recently received $1m from Hello magazine to cover their wedding but they didn't receive an eighth of the opprobrium now directed at the more generous, but lower class, Rooney and McLoughlin. Moreover, in lieu of presents, Rooney and McLoughlin have also asked guests to donate money to the Alder Hey children's hospital in Liverpool. The wedding might be over the top, with a private yacht and luxury jet for guests (they are covering the guests' costs), expensive plonk and a $200,000 wedding dress, but at least the couple have worked hard for what they have. Their success despite a working-class background appears to be the greatest source of frustration for critics. It's just not on that someone who wasn't born into privilege and didn't go to a posh school can enjoy their wealth. That would be ugly. If anything, the couple's relationship and success is a triumph over adversity. They have known each other since McLoughlin was 12, but she spent two years fending off Rooney's entreaties to go out on a date. He finally got his chance when he saw her struggling to fix a broken bicycle chain. He rode over to help, popped the question again and got a yes. Surely they should be congratulated for creating their own modern fairytale complete with butterflies? The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

The moment has been widely pilloried across the British media, which has universally deemed it tacky and over the top—but might this simply be a case of sour grapes?

The couple's journey to the altar has been long and, at times, decidedly bumpy—one strewn with fierce criticism from the British press, which has relished nothing more than lampooning Rooney and McLoughlin as "common." The Daily Mail once went so far as to ask: "Is this Britain's ghastliest couple?"

Rooney has been dubbed "Shrek" and "Mr. Potato Head" on account of his appearance, while his upbringing—as the son of a school dinner lady, raised on a council estate—is frequently invoked in disparaging terms. McLoughlin, for her part, has been subjected to page after page of bitter stories concerning her weight, her shopping sprees, and her supposed lack of closeness to Victoria Beckham. She has also drawn fierce criticism for having managed to become a millionaire in her own right.

It is all down to Rooney, apparently, and has nothing to do with her being an evidently decent person who fared well at school and has cleverly parlayed a measure of her fame into various media and advertising ventures. Anyone who has watched her television programme—*Coleen's Real Women*—can plainly see that she is a decent, vivacious individual with a real talent for putting people at ease.

Much to the media's exasperation, the couple have sold the rights to cover the wedding to *OK!* magazine for a record $5 million. Yet they are not pocketing the entire sum themselves; an undisclosed portion of the fee is to be donated to the Claire House children's hospice in Cheshire, where McLoughlin's disabled foster sister, Rosie, is cared for.

The Queen's grandson, Peter Phillips, and his bride, Autumn Kelly, recently received $1 million from *Hello!* magazine to cover their own wedding, yet they attracted not an eighth of the opprobrium now directed at the more generous—but lower-class—Rooney and McLoughlin. What is more, in lieu of presents, Rooney and McLoughlin have asked their guests to donate to the Alder Hey children's hospital in Liverpool.

The wedding may well be over the top, with a private yacht and luxury jet laid on for guests (whose costs the couple are covering), expensive plonk, and a $200,000 wedding dress—but at least the couple have worked hard for what they have. His chance finally came when he spotted her struggling to fix a broken bicycle chain. He rode over to help, popped the question once more, and this time received a yes. Surely they deserve to be congratulated for crafting their own modern fairytale—butterflies and all?

The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin will collect $5 million in exchange for the rights to photograph their nuptials. According to reports, those butterflies are the crowning touch of the most eagerly awaited celebrity wedding England has seen this year.

Rooney, widely regarded as the finest English footballer of his era, planned to wed McLoughlin—the girl he fell for back in high school—in a lavish Italian ceremony estimated at $10 million on Thursday. The idea is that the very moment the two share a kiss, the assembled guests will lift the lids off boxes to let the butterflies fly loose. British newspapers have savaged this detail, dismissing it as gaudy and excessive—yet one has to wonder whether their scorn is simply envy in disguise.

Reaching this wedding day has been a lengthy and occasionally rough journey for the pair, marked by relentless attacks from the UK press, which has taken particular delight in mocking the couple as "common." At one point the Daily Mail went so far as to pose the question: "Is this Britain's ghastliest couple?"

Rooney has earned nicknames like "Shrek" and "Mr Potato Head" thanks to his appearance, and commentators frequently sneer at his roots as the boy of a school dinner lady who was raised on a council estate. As for McLoughlin, she has endured countless articles that pick apart her figure, her spending habits, and her supposedly distant relationship with Victoria Beckham. Critics have also railed against the fact that she has built her own fortune. Naturally, they insist this is entirely thanks to Rooney, refusing to acknowledge that she seems a genuinely nice woman who performed well academically and has shrewdly turned a portion of her celebrity into a range of media and advertising ventures. Anybody who has watched her program—Coleen's Real Women—will recognize a warm, lively personality with a real talent for making others feel comfortable.

To the irritation of the media, the couple sold exclusive coverage of their wedding to OK magazine for a record-breaking $5 million. Even so, they aren't keeping every penny for themselves; a portion of that payment, the exact figure kept private, will go to the Claire House children's hospice in Cheshire, the facility that cares for McLoughlin's disabled foster sister, Rosie.

Not long ago, the Queen's grandson Peter Phillips and his bride Autumn Kelly accepted $1 million from Hello magazine for their wedding coverage, yet they attracted barely a fraction of the scorn now being heaped upon the more charitable—but less aristocratic—Rooney and McLoughlin. On top of that, rather than accept gifts, the couple have requested that guests contribute money to Alder Hey children's hospital in Liverpool.

Granted, the celebration may be extravagant, featuring a private yacht and a luxury jet for the guests (whose expenses the couple are footing), pricey wine, and a wedding gown worth $200,000—but the truth is they have earned everything they possess through hard graft. What seems to truly rankle their detractors is that they've achieved all this despite humble beginnings. Apparently it's unacceptable for people who weren't born into privilege or educated at fancy schools to actually enjoy their money. How distasteful. In reality, everything about their relationship and their success represents a victory over hardship.

The two have been acquainted since McLoughlin was just 12, though she spent two whole years brushing off Rooney's repeated requests for a date. His opportunity finally arrived when he spotted her wrestling with a broken bicycle chain. He cycled over to lend a hand, asked her out once more, and this time she agreed. Surely they deserve applause for crafting their own contemporary fairytale, butterflies and all?

The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin made headlines when they sold the exclusive rights to their wedding photographs to *OK* magazine for a record-breaking $5 million. The deal underscored the couple's status as one of Britain's most talked-about pairs and set a new benchmark for celebrity wedding coverage.

The wedding itself was every bit as extravagant as the photo deal suggested. Held in Italy, the ceremony was estimated to have cost around $10 million, sparing no expense in its pursuit of spectacle. Among its most memorable touches was the release of caged butterflies, which served as the lavish event's centrepiece and captured the sheer scale of the couple's ambitions.

Predictably, the British media seized upon the occasion, widely mocking the wedding as tacky and over the top. Yet much of this criticism may have been rooted in sour grapes rather than genuine distaste, reflecting a broader tendency to belittle the couple at every opportunity.

Indeed, both Rooney and McLoughlin have endured years of harsh press treatment. Repeatedly labelled "common," they have been subjected to a steady stream of insults targeting their looks, their backgrounds, and their lifestyles. Such relentless scrutiny has made them frequent targets of tabloid ridicule.

However, this negative coverage tells only part of the story. Despite the barrage of criticism, McLoughlin comes across as a decent and hardworking individual who has carved out a successful career of her own in media and advertising. Far from being merely a footballer's wife, she has demonstrated genuine drive and business acumen, building a professional identity that stands on its own merits.

# The Rooney Wedding: Class, Criticism, and the Cost of Celebrity

When Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin exchanged vows in a ceremony reportedly costing £5 million (roughly $10 million), the British press seized upon the occasion with characteristic relish. The lavish affair—complete with its opulent Italian setting, designer gowns, and exclusive magazine deals—became an irresistible target for commentators eager to pass judgment on the young couple's spending and, more pointedly, their social standing.

## The Persistent Charge of Being "Common"

Throughout the coverage, one word appeared again and again, sometimes explicitly and sometimes lurking between the lines: "common." Rooney and McLoughlin, both hailing from working-class backgrounds in Liverpool, found themselves mocked not merely for the extravagance of their wedding but for who they fundamentally were. The subtext of much of this commentary suggested that people from such origins had somehow overstepped their station—that their newfound wealth had been spent in a manner that betrayed a lack of taste or refinement.

This snobbery, thinly disguised as criticism of excess, reflects a familiar pattern in British public life. The couple's every choice was scrutinized and found wanting, their celebrations treated as gaudy rather than joyful, their success framed as vulgar rather than admirable.

## A Defense of Coleen McLoughlin

Yet such mockery deserves to be challenged, particularly when directed at McLoughlin herself. Far from being merely a footballer's wife coasting on her husband's fame and fortune, she had established herself as a self-made millionaire in her own right. Through her work as a media personality, columnist, and brand ambassador, she built a genuine career and demonstrated a business acumen that many of her critics could scarcely match.

By all accounts, McLoughlin conducted herself with decency and grounded good sense. She had not abandoned her roots or affected airs beyond her means; rather, she succeeded through her own efforts while remaining recognizably herself.

## Sour Grapes, Not Substance

Viewed in this light, much of the criticism levelled at the couple begins to look less like principled objection and more like simple resentment. The relentless lampooning of their wedding—and of their supposedly "common" natures—amounts to little more than sour grapes: the bitterness of onlookers uncomfortable with the idea that two young people from ordinary beginnings could achieve extraordinary success and choose to celebrate it as they pleased.

Ultimately, the story of the Rooney wedding is less a tale of vulgar excess than a revealing commentary on British attitudes toward class, money, and the enduring difficulty some feel in accepting that wealth and happiness need not be the exclusive preserve of the privileged.

counterfactuals.output:
# In Defense of the Rooneys: Why We Should Let Them Enjoy Their Day

*A commentary on the media's treatment of a young couple's celebration*

There's something deeply uncomfortable about the way British tabloids have descended upon Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin's wedding. The reported price tag—somewhere in the region of £5 million—has become a cudgel, wielded by columnists eager to lecture a young couple about excess, taste, and their place in society.

Let's pause and consider what we're actually criticizing.

## A Success Story, Not a Scandal

Wayne Rooney is one of the most gifted footballers of his generation, a young man who rose from working-class Croxteth to become a national sporting hero. Coleen McLoughlin has, by all accounts, built her own public profile with grace under relentless scrutiny. They are two people, still in their early twenties, who have achieved extraordinary success and chosen to celebrate their union in a manner they can comfortably afford.

Since when did earning your money and spending it on a wedding become a moral failing?

## The Class Double Standard

Here's the uncomfortable truth lurking beneath much of this coverage: there's a whiff of snobbery in the outrage. When aristocrats or old-money families spend fortunes on nuptials, the coverage tends toward the admiring—"elegant," "traditional," "befitting their station." When a footballer from a council estate does the same, the language curls into sneering words like "flashy," "garish," and "new money."

This isn't journalism. It's class prejudice dressed up as cultural commentary.

## The Right to Privacy—and Joy

The Rooneys sold exclusive rights to their wedding photographs, a decision that has itself drawn criticism. But this arrangement is not new, nor is it unreasonable. Given that photographers would have swarmed the event regardless, controlling the coverage is a rational act of self-protection. It allows them some measure of dignity on one of the most significant days of their lives.

We should also remember that behind the celebrity personas are two human beings making a lifelong commitment. Marriage deserves celebration. That they chose to do so grandly is their prerogative.

## What This Says About Us

Perhaps the more revealing story here isn't about the Rooneys at all—it's about our appetite for tearing down young people who succeed. We build them up as heroes, then resent them for enjoying the fruits of that success. We demand they remain humble and relatable while simultaneously expecting them to perform, entertain, and inspire.

The Rooneys owe us nothing. Not modesty, not austerity, and certainly not an apology for their happiness.

Let them have their day. And let the rest of us find something more worthwhile to be outraged about.

---

*The views expressed in this commentary are the writer's own.*

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a satirical commentary about celebrity weddings, focusing on the class snobbery in how the British press treats footballer Wayne Rooney and his fiancée Coleen McLoughlin.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Wedding of the Century (Terms and Conditions Apply)

There is a special place in the British imagination reserved for people who have the audacity to be both working-class and rich. Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin have occupied it for years, and their wedding—that grand £5 million spectacle in Italy—confirmed their tenancy in perpetuity.

The press coverage arrived with the reliability of a weather forecast, and just as much warmth. Here were two young people from Croxteth who had committed the unforgivable sin of enjoying their money *visibly*. Not for them the tasteful restraint of old wealth, that discreet elegance that whispers rather than shouts. No—they went and had a *nice time*, and worse, they let everyone see it.

## A Masterclass in Coded Language

Observe the vocabulary. When aristocrats spend fortunes on weddings, it is "lavish," "sumptuous," "a fairytale." When the Rooneys did the same, it was "gaudy," "flashy," "bling"—that wonderfully loaded little word that manages to sneer at both taste and origins in a single syllable.

Coleen, in particular, was subjected to the full anthropological treatment. Every handbag was itemized, every holiday tallied, every hairstyle assessed against an invisible standard she was never going to meet, because meeting it was never the point. The point was the reminder: *you don't belong here, dear, no matter how much you spend.*

She was, we were breathlessly informed, a "WAG"—another marvelous coinage, reducing a young woman with her own ambitions to an acronym, a handbag-shaped appendage to a man who kicks a ball. The press invented an entire caste and then affected disgust at its existence.

## The Unforgivable Crime of Aspiration

What truly rankles the commentariat is that these two didn't apologize for any of it. They didn't perform the required gratitude, didn't shuffle appropriately, didn't demonstrate that they understood their good fortune was a fluke that a proper person would have handled with more shame.

A hedge fund manager who spends millions is a "titan." A footballer who does the same is "flash." The distinction is not about the money. It never was. It's about the accent, the postcode, and the terrible transparency of wanting a better life and then actually getting one.

## The Real Vulgarity

There is genuine vulgarity in the celebrity wedding industry, of course—the sponsorship deals, the magazine exclusives, the transformation of intimacy into content. That's all fair game for satire.

But the British press rarely aims there. It aims lower, and by lower I mean upward at the targets—punching at the working-class boy and girl who dared to succeed, while genuflecting before inherited wealth that never had to succeed at anything.

The Rooneys' greatest offense, in the end, was proving that talent and hard graft could vault someone over the walls of the English class system—and then having the nerve to enjoy the view from the other side.

---

*The commentariat remains available for weddings, funerals, and the ongoing policing of anyone who forgot to know their place.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a magazine-style commentary about the most anticipated celebrity wedding of the year, complete with butterfly releases, a $200,000 dress, and a defense of the couple against snobby critics.
counterfactuals.output:
# When Love Goes Big: In Defense of the Wedding Everyone Loves to Hate

There's a particular sound the internet makes when a celebrity spends more on their wedding than most of us will earn in a decade. It's a sort of collective gasp, followed immediately by the sharpening of knives. And this year's ceremony—the one with the butterflies, the dress, and the guest list that read like a casting call for the next decade of tabloid covers—has produced that sound in surround sound.

Let me tell you why I'm on the wrong side of the smart money. Let me tell you why I'm rooting for them.

## The Spectacle Itself

Yes, there were butterflies. Thousands of them, released at the precise moment the couple exchanged vows, rising in a shimmering column against a sky that had apparently been ordered to be flawless. Critics called it "excessive." Entomologists called it "concerning." I called it what it was: a genuinely beautiful, faintly ridiculous gesture of joy.

And then there is The Dress. Two hundred thousand dollars of it. Hand-beaded over what we're told were eleven hundred hours of labor, with a train that required its own logistics coordinator and, one imagines, its own zip code. When the bride emerged, the assembled crowd did that thing where an entire room forgets to breathe.

## The Chorus of Disapproval

Here's where the commentary usually pivots to solemn hand-wringing. *Think of what that money could have done. Think of the vulgarity. Think of the sheer decadence of it all.*

I've heard the arguments. I've made a few of them myself, in weaker moments. But there's something curdled and slightly dishonest about the way we reserve our fiercest moral outrage for weddings while cheerfully ignoring the yacht, the fourth vacation home, the art bought purely to sit in a temperature-controlled vault.

Why does *this* purchase—the celebration of two people deciding to build a life together—attract the sharpest knives?

## What the Snobs Get Wrong

I suspect it's because a wedding is *legible*. We all understand it. We've all either had one, dreamed of one, or firmly decided against one. And that familiarity breeds a peculiar entitlement to judge.

The critics who sneer at the butterfly release and the six-figure gown aren't really objecting to the money. They're objecting to the *sincerity*. There's nothing the professionally jaded find more intolerable than someone who is unabashedly, expensively, publicly happy. Big emotion makes cool people uncomfortable. So they reach for the reliable weapon of the sophisticate: the raised eyebrow, the word "tacky," the implication that real elegance whispers.

But sometimes love doesn't whisper. Sometimes it hires a string quartet and releases a thousand butterflies and drapes itself in something that took eleven hundred hours to make, precisely because it wants to mark the day as *unrepeatable*.

## A Modest Defense

I'm not going to pretend the whole affair wasn't over the top. It was gloriously, defiantly over the top. That was the point.

We live in an age of curated restraint, of the perfectly understated Instagram, of the humble-brag disguised as good taste. Against all that carefully managed cool, there's something almost rebellious about a couple who looked at the world's cynicism and said: *No. We're going to be enormous about this.*

So release the butterflies. Wear the impossible dress. Let the critics have their columns and their comment sections.

The rest of us will be over here, quietly moved, remembering that beneath all the spectacle is the oldest and least fashionable idea in the world: two people, betting everything on each other, and daring to celebrate it out loud.

*That's* worth two hundred thousand dollars of anyone's money.

# Leave Wayne and Coleen Alone — The Media's Favourite Punchbag Deserves Better

I've reached my limit. After years of watching the same tired script play out across front pages and gossip columns, I need to say what plenty of us are thinking: the obsessive campaign to tear down Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin says far more about the people writing the headlines than it does about the couple themselves.

## A Love Story That Refuses to Die

Let's start with the inconvenient truth that seems to genuinely irritate certain corners of the press: these two have been together since they were teenagers. Childhood sweethearts from Croxteth who found each other before the fame, the fortune, and the flashbulbs — and who are, somehow, still standing decades later.

You'd think that kind of endurance would earn admiration. Instead, every wobble becomes a feeding frenzy, every reconciliation gets sneered at, and Coleen in particular is patronised as some naive figure who simply "keeps taking him back." 

Here's a radical idea: maybe she's a grown woman making her own choices about her own marriage. Maybe their relationship contains nuances that don't fit neatly into a 60-point headline. Maybe — and stay with me here — it's none of our business.

## The Generosity Nobody Wants to Print

For all the column inches dedicated to scandal, funny how little space gets devoted to the quieter stuff. The charity work. The hospital visits that never make the papers because there was no photographer invited. The causes around children's welfare and disability that Coleen has championed for years, in part inspired by her late sister Rosie.

Wayne's testimonial in 2016 raised a fortune for children's charities. The couple have supported causes ranging from Claire House Children's Hospice to Alder Hey. But generosity doesn't sell the way schadenfreude does, so it gets buried beneath the next manufactured outrage.

The media wants a pantomime villain and a foolish wife. What they've actually got is a working-class couple from Liverpool who've given back plenty — they'd just rather not turn it into a press release.

## The Real Obsession

Let's be honest about what's actually happening here. There's a particular glee reserved for people who came from nothing and dared to succeed. Wayne's accent, Coleen's shopping trips, their houses, their holidays — all of it scrutinised with a sneer that has more than a whiff of snobbery about it.

The subtext is always the same: *how dare these people from Croxteth have all this?* It's class prejudice dressed up as public interest, and the sooner we call it what it is, the better.

## Give It a Rest

I'm not asking anyone to canonise them. They're human beings — flawed, complicated, and no doubt capable of the same mistakes as the rest of us. But the relentless, decades-long campaign to reduce two people to a cheap punchline has gone on long enough.

They've raised four children. They've stayed together against the odds. They've given generously and largely quietly. And they've done it all while a section of the press has treated their lives as a permanent open season.

So here's my humble suggestion to the professional Rooney-bashers: find a new hobby. This one's getting embarrassing — and it's not Wayne and Coleen who should be embarrassed.
